code.title: Error budget and burn policy
code.python:
# Error budget: 1,000,000 requests, SLO 99.9% -> 1000 bad requests allowed
total, slo_permille = 1000000, 999
budget = total * (1000 - slo_permille) // 1000   # allowed bad requests
bad_per_day = [50, 30, 200, 20, 10, 300, 40, 0, 60, 100, 250]
used = 0
print("budget:", budget, "bad requests")
for day, bad in enumerate(bad_per_day, 1):
    used += bad
    left = budget - used
    # policy agreed in advance: ship / slow down / freeze
    if left <= 0:
        state = "FREEZE"
    elif left < budget // 4:
        state = "SLOW"
    else:
        state = "SHIP"
    print("day", day, "used", used, "left", left, state)

followUps:
Start from what users need, then check it against history. Pick the SLIs that match the user journey (for checkout: success rate and latency), measure a few weeks of real data, and set the SLO slightly below what you already achieve. If last month was 99.95%, a 99.9% SLO is realistic; 99.99% would leave only 4.3 minutes a month.

For a brand-new service with no data, begin loose (say 99.5%), publish it as provisional and tighten it after one or two review cycles. Also check that it does not exceed the SLOs of your dependencies.

An unspent budget means the SLO is probably too strict or the team is too cautious, so use the slack on purpose. If a 99.9% service keeps finishing at 99.99%, you are paying for reliability users cannot notice.

Options: ship faster, run chaos experiments, do risky migrations, or loosen the SLO to match real need. A budget that is always full is a sign to take more risk, not a trophy.

Keep mitigating, widen the search and bring in more people, because rollback was only one hypothesis. Re-check that the rollback really finished and the old version is serving. Then work the request path: dependencies, database locks or saturation, expired certificates, quota limits, a third party outage.

Useful moves: fail over to another zone, turn off the newest feature flag, shed load, scale up, or serve a degraded page. Add a subject expert to the call and keep the status updates going every 20 minutes even with no news.

Do a short, explicit handover so the new IC knows everything the old one does, and say it out loud on the call. After four hours people are tired and decisions get worse, so swap proactively.

  • Old IC summarises: impact, current theory, what was tried, who owns what, next update time.
  • New IC repeats it back and says "I am now IC".
  • The scribe records the time of the handover.

The old IC stays reachable for questions, then rests.

Treat it as a system question first: why was the rule easy to break and why did nothing stop it? A rule that depends on memory fails eventually, so add a guardrail such as a CI check, a required approval or a permission limit.

If someone knowingly ignored a clear rule, that is a performance conversation and it happens in private with their manager, not in the postmortem document. The postmortem stays about the system, so people keep reporting honestly. Punishing people hides the next incident.

Rank actions by risk removed per effort, and be willing to say no to the rest. Ask three questions: would this have prevented or shortened this incident, how likely is the same gap elsewhere, and how many hours does it cost?

Example: a 2-hour alert tweak that would have cut detection from 30 to 5 minutes beats a 3-week rewrite of a rarely failing job. Prefer prevent over detect over mitigate, keep 3 to 6 actions, and drop items nobody will own.

code.title: Little's law and pool exhaustion
code.python:
# Little's law: in-flight requests L = arrival rate x time in system
rate = 200          # requests per second
pool = 100          # connection pool size
for latency_ms in [250, 500, 2500]:
    in_flight = rate * latency_ms // 1000
    status = "POOL EXHAUSTED" if in_flight > pool else "ok"
    print("rate", rate, "rps, latency", latency_ms, "ms -> in flight", in_flight, status)
# sizing: pool needed for 250 ms with 30% headroom
need = rate * 250 // 1000
print("pool with 30% headroom:", need * 130 // 100)

followUps:
They describe the same effect from two sides. Little's law tells you how many requests are inside the system, while the 1/(1-rho) curve tells you why latency W climbs as utilisation rho approaches 100%.

For a simple queue the average time is roughly service time / (1 - rho). At 50% busy that is 2x service time, at 90% it is 10x, at 99% it is 100x. Feed that growing W into L = lambda x W and in-flight requests explode, which is why pools and queues overflow suddenly. Keep utilisation well below the knee.

Multiply the queries per second that need the database by the average time each holds a connection, then add headroom. If 400 queries per second each hold a connection for 20 ms, L = 400 x 0.020 = 8 connections in use on average.

Add headroom for bursts and slow queries, say 2x, giving 16. Then check the database limit: connections from all app instances add up, so with 10 instances each pool of 16 means 160 connections on the server. A bigger pool does not help if the database is already the bottleneck.

Usually the database, because it is stateful and cannot simply be cloned. Stateless web and API servers scale out in minutes, but a primary database has one writer, a fixed connection limit and a cache that must be warm.

Close behind are things with hidden limits: third party rate limits, NAT gateway ports, cloud quotas, a single hot key in the cache and connection pool exhaustion. That is why the load test must push the whole path, not one service, and find the knee before the event does.

Cloud load balancers scale their own capacity gradually, so a sudden spike can get errors while it grows. For a known event, ask the provider to pre-warm it, or open a support case with the expected request rate and traffic shape.

You can also ramp traffic up with a load test over 30 to 60 minutes beforehand so it scales naturally. Check its limits too, such as new connections per second and target counts. Not every provider needs a request; read the current docs for yours.

code.title: Toil payback ranking
code.python:
# Toil payback: weeks until the automation pays for itself
# each task: (name, hours of toil per week, hours to build the fix)
tasks = [("restart stuck job", 3, 6), ("renew certs by hand", 1, 10),
         ("grant user access", 5, 20), ("clean old logs", 2, 6)]
week_hours = 40
total = sum(t[1] for t in tasks)
print("toil:", total, "of", week_hours, "hours a week =", total * 100 // week_hours, "percent")
rows = []
for name, per_week, build in tasks:
    payback = (build + per_week - 1) // per_week   # round up to whole weeks
    rows.append((payback, name))
rows.sort()                                        # shortest payback first
for payback, name in rows:
    print("payback", payback, "weeks:", name)

followUps:
Automation is wrong when the task is rare, changing or risky, so the build and upkeep cost more than the time saved. A task done twice a year for 30 minutes will never pay back a 3-day script.

Another case is automating a broken process: a script that approves every access request fast just makes a bad control faster. Better to remove the cause or make it self-service. Also watch for brittle scripts that fail silently and need more care than the manual job did.

Measure where the time goes, then remove the biggest items first. Say the team spends 28 of 40 hours on toil; label tickets for two weeks and rank the categories.

  1. Eliminate the cause for the top item (fix the flaky job, not restart it).
  2. Make requests self-service for the next.
  3. Automate the rest by shortest payback.

Protect time for this in the sprint, say 20%, and stop taking new toil without leadership agreeing. Re-measure monthly.

The best finding is one that changes a design, such as a hidden single point of failure. In my capstone, killing one pod looked fine, but the whole checkout stalled because the app had a single database connection string with no timeout and no retry.

The hypothesis was that traffic would stay above 99% success. It dropped to 80%. The fix was a timeout, a retry with backoff and a second replica, and the re-run passed. A good result is a gap found cheaply on a Tuesday instead of at 2 a.m.

Speak in terms of risk and money, and start small. Explain that failures will happen anyway, and the choice is whether you find them in a planned test with the team watching, or in an outage at 2 a.m.

Offer a safe first step: one pod in staging, 5 minutes, automatic abort on an alert, and the manager can stop it at any time. Show the result, then grow slowly. Say plainly that you will not test when the error budget is nearly spent.

Answer honestly with your own story: name the work you actually did, such as owning SLOs, writing runbooks, running on-call, building pipelines or shared tooling, and say which label it matches best. Do not claim a title you have not held.

A simple structure: where you started (for example, deploys), what you took on (alerts, incident roles, a postmortem habit), a result with a number (page count down from 30 to 12 a week), and where you want to grow. Interviewers care about the behaviour, not the title.

DORA metrics measure delivery speed and stability, and SLOs measure what users experience, so they balance each other. DORA has deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate and time to restore.

Fast deployment is good only if the SLO holds. Example: if you deploy 10 times a day and the change failure rate rises, the error budget burns faster and the policy slows releases. Time to restore also matches how fast you stop the burn. Use both so speed does not beat reliability.

Count how many pages led to action, and treat the rest as defects. For each alert, review weekly: was it actionable, did it need a human right now, and did the runbook help?

Useful numbers: pages per shift (target about 2 or fewer), percentage actionable (aim above 90%), time to acknowledge, and repeat pages for the same cause. If 20 of 100 pages needed no action, that is 80% actionable and those 20 should be deleted, merged or made tickets.

Four people is too few for a healthy 24/7 rotation, since each would be on call one week in four with little recovery. First reduce the load: remove noisy alerts, automate the top fixes and page only on user-facing symptoms.

Then consider options: business-hours-only paging for lower tier services, a follow-the-sun handover with another team, or borrowing engineers from a related team. Pay for out-of-hours work, allow time off after a bad night, and tell leadership the risk plainly.

The hardest bug was a deploy that passed in kind but failed on AWS because the pods could not reach the database. The cause was a security group that allowed the node group but not the pod network setting I used.

I found it by testing from a debug pod with a plain connection check rather than reading app logs, which only showed timeouts. I fixed the rule in Terraform and added a smoke test to the pipeline so the check runs on every deploy. It taught me to test the network path first.

I would reverse starting with EKS for a project this small. A managed Kubernetes cluster cost most of the budget and took the longest to build, while an app on a simple container service would have met the same goals.

I picked it because it matched what jobs ask for, and that was a fair reason, but I should have written down the trade-off. Next time I would start with the smaller option, record a decision note, and move to Kubernetes only when the need appears.

code.title: Serial and parallel availability
code.python:
# Availability math in parts per million (ppm); 1,000,000 ppm = 100%
M = 1000000
def serial(parts):                 # every part must work: multiply
    s = M
    for p in parts:
        s = s * p // M
    return s
def parallel(p, n):                # n copies: fails only if all fail
    fail = M
    for _ in range(n):
        fail = fail * (M - p) // M
    return M - fail
lb, api, db = 999900, 995000, 999500
one = serial([lb, api, db])
two = serial([lb, parallel(api, 2), db])
minutes = 43200                    # one 30-day month
print("one API copy :", one, "ppm, downtime", (M - one) * minutes // M, "min/month")
print("two API copies:", two, "ppm, downtime", (M - two) * minutes // M, "min/month")

followUps:
Your best case cannot exceed that dependency's availability, because serial parts multiply. If the checkout SLO is 99.95% and a payment provider offers 99.9%, calls that must succeed in real time cap you at about 99.9%.

Options: make the call asynchronous with a queue and retry, add a second provider as fallback, cache or degrade (accept the order and charge later), or lower the SLO honestly. Put the dependency in the error budget math and measure it separately.

Go multi-region when a whole region loss would cost more than running two, or when the SLO or law demands it. A 99.95% target can usually be met with multiple zones in one region.

Multi-region adds big costs: data replication delay, conflict handling, traffic routing and double the testing. Choose active-passive first with a measured RTO and RPO, and use active-active only if the business needs near-zero downtime. Practise the failover, as an untested plan fails.

Kubernetes waits longer after each crash: the delay starts at 10 seconds and doubles (10, 20, 40, 80, 160 seconds) up to a cap of 5 minutes. It resets after the container runs fine for about 10 minutes.

That means a pod can look quiet between restarts, so read kubectl logs --previous instead of waiting. After a fix, the pod may still take up to 5 minutes to retry; deleting the pod forces a fresh start.

Distroless images have no shell, so you attach a temporary debug container instead: kubectl debug -it POD --image=busybox --target=CONTAINER. It shares the process namespace, so you can inspect processes, network and files through /proc.

Other options: debug a copy of the pod with --copy-to and a different image, or build a debug variant of the image for staging. Never ship a shell into production just for convenience.

Pin the audience, the repository and the branch or environment. The token carries claims, and the trust policy must match them exactly or anyone could assume the role.

For GitHub Actions that means aud equals the cloud audience, and sub equals something like repo:ORG/REPO:ref:refs/heads/main or repo:ORG/REPO:environment:production. Avoid wildcards on the repository. Using the environment claim lets required reviewers gate production.

Use one role per account and environment, each with its own narrow trust policy, instead of one powerful role. The pipeline assumes the role for the target account in each deploy job.

Example: a dev role trusts the main branch, while the prod role trusts only the production environment and has deploy permissions for that account only. Keep accounts separate, avoid chaining roles across them with broad rights, and log every assumption for audit.
